newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russia's Nemtsov is champion of market reforms.
newsitem.headline: Russia's Nemtsov is champion of market reforms.

text.p: Boris Nemtsov, the 37-year-old first deputy prime minister appointed fuel and energy minister on Thursday, is a popular champion of liberal reforms and a potential successor to President Boris Yeltsin.
His telegenic good looks, mop of dark curly hair and easy charm made him a household name across Russia even when he was still only a regional governor.

Yeltsin, who has long admired Nemtsov's youthful energy, drafted him into the government last month to oversee the restructuring of natural monopolies like gas, electricity and railways and also tackle housing reform.
"You can already tip him for president," Yeltsin said of Nemtsov as long as three years ago.

Nemtsov is rumoured to be behind the 66-year-old president's latest crusade against corruption and he also played a role in watering down a controversial union treaty with neighbouring Belarus, which has been resisting market reforms.
Earlier on Thursday, anticipating the announcement on Nemtsov, Yeltsin spoke of the need to promote younger people to safeguard Russia's reform process.

The move was a new warning to seasoned Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin, who has seen control of economic reforms shift away from him under the reshuffle and whose hopes of succeeding Yeltsin in the year 2000 appear to be receding.

A recent survey by the Public Opinion Foundation named Nemtsov as the most trusted Russian politician, ahead of other potential future rivals for the presidency like populist Moscow mayor Yuri Luzhkov and former security chief Alexander Lebed.
Nemtsov has made clear in a book soon to hit Russia's bookstores that he wants to go down in history as a man who made life better for ordinary Russians.

"My success will be absolute when people start living better and, if my investment in this success is visible, when people say 'it was so-and-so in the Nemtsov times and now it is different'," he wrote in "The Provincial".
But Nemtsov also speaks of himself as a political kamikaze, referring to the Japanese pilots who went on missions knowing they would die.
"Russia is a cruel country. It does not pardon you even for the good things you did for it. People do not thank you here."

One of his first steps as first deputy prime minister was a pledge to drive foreign cars out of the Kremlin car pool and to make officials ride Russian-made cars from his home town of Nizhny Novgorod.
For all his youth, Nemtsov has shown himself a tough politician, standing up to local and national criticism of his radical policies.
When ultra-nationalist Vladimir Zhirinovsky called him a "scumbag" and threw orange juice at him during a live television debate in 1995, Nemtsov had no hesitation in replying in kind.

Born in the Black Sea resort of Sochi, Nemtsov graduated in radio physics from Gorky University in 1981 and worked as an engineer in the city. He took his first steps in politics during the Soviet era as an environmental campaigner.
In 1990, at the age of 30, he was elected a deputy to the Russian Federation Supreme Soviet and then moved on to the Supreme Soviet of the Soviet Union.
Yeltsin appointed him head of the Nizhny Novgorod administration in November 1991 as the Soviet Union broke up.
He was elected to a second term in December 1995 and again, comfortably, last autumn.
Nemtsov made a media splash when Nizhny Novgorod region was the first in Russia to auction off small shops and firms, and to sell municipally-owned trucking operations to drivers.

In 1993, launching a pilot project with a unit of the World Bank, a state farm near Nizhny Novgorod made history as the first in Russia to go private since Josef Stalin's brutal collectivisation drive in the 1930s.
Nemtsov, like Yeltsin before his recent heart trouble, is a keen tennis player. He is married and has one daughter.
